b: After eleven chapters about the whole world, the Bible narrows to one man. Abram is living in Haran, having come from Ur with his father Terah, when the LORD says to him: "Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you" (Genesis 12:1). With the command come three promises: a great nation, a land, and a blessing that will reach "all the families of the earth" (Genesis 12:3). He is seventy-five, his wife Sarai is barren, and he is told to leave everything behind. Abram goes.

The promise is repeated and deepened. In Genesis 15 God takes him outside, tells him to count the stars, and says his descendants will be as many. Abram "believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). That one verse becomes the center of Paul's argument in Romans 4 and Galatians 3: Abraham was put right with God by trusting, long before the law of Moses, and so all who trust God as he did are his children.

In Genesis 17 God makes the covenant formal. He changes the names to Abraham ("father of many") and Sarah, promises to be God to him and to his offspring, and gives circumcision as the sign. A covenant in the ancient world was a binding relationship with promises and obligations. This one is mostly promise: God does the main work.

The date of Abraham is debated, but most place him early in the second millennium BC, perhaps between 2000 and 1800 BC. What matters for the story is the shape. After Babel, God does not give up on the nations. He chooses one family so that through them the blessing may reach all the others.

Genesis 10 lists the descendants of Noah's sons as the family of nations, in a table of seventy names. Genesis 11 then steps back to tell how they came to be spread out and speaking different languages. The people settle on a plain in Shinar, which is the region of Babylonia, and decide to build a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, "that we may make a name for ourselves and not be scattered over the face of all the earth" (Genesis 11:4).

The two motives are the whole story. They want a name for themselves, which is pride, and they want to avoid being scattered, which is a refusal of God's command to fill the earth. The tower is probably a ziggurat, the stepped temple-tower common in Mesopotamia. Archaeologists have found the remains of many of them. The narrator has some fun with the scene: the people are building a tower to reach the heavens, and God has to come down to see it (Genesis 11:5).

God confuses their speech, and they stop building. The city is called Babel, which sounds like the Hebrew word for confused, though in the Akkadian language of Babylon the same word, Babilu, meant "gate of God." The great monument to human greatness becomes a symbol of human failure.

The story also sets up everything that follows. The nations are now divided and drifting, and the next chapter introduces a man whom God will call out of that world to bless "all the families of the earth." The reversal comes at Pentecost, when people from every nation hear the apostles' message in their own languages (Acts 2:5-11), and it is completed in the vision of Revelation 7:9, where a crowd from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne.

The Jews carried into Babylon did not become slaves in chains. They were settled in communities along the canals, such as the one at Tel Abib by the Kebar River, where Ezekiel lived, and many farmed, built houses and engaged in trade. Archaeologists have found cuneiform tablets from this period that name Judean families in a town called Al-Yahudu, which means "Judah-town." Still, they were exiles, far from Jerusalem and the temple, and they were not sure that God could be found anywhere else. Psalm 137 captures the mood: "By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion."

God sent prophets to them. Ezekiel saw visions of the glory of the LORD leaving the temple and then, in later chapters, returning. In the valley of dry bones he is told to prophesy to a field of skeletons, and they stand up as an army. God explains: "these bones are the whole house of Israel" who say that their hope is lost, and he promises to open their graves and "put My Spirit in you and you will live" (Ezekiel 37:11-14). Daniel, taken to Babylon young, rose in the Babylonian and Persian courts while keeping his faith, and kept praying three times a day toward Jerusalem even when it was illegal (Daniel 6:10).

The exile also did something to the Jewish people. It cured them of open idolatry, which was never again their main problem. It produced the gathering of Scripture: scribes copied and edited the older books, and the synagogue, a place of reading and prayer that did not require a temple, probably grew up in this period. It also gave a new word to the vocabulary of hope. When Isaiah 40 opens, "Comfort, comfort My people," the exile is what it is speaking to.

Within a single generation, the fall bears its first terrible fruit. Cain and Abel bring offerings to God, and God accepts Abel's but not Cain's. The text does not say precisely why, though the New Testament says Abel offered "by faith" (Hebrews 11:4), and John says Cain's deeds were evil (1 John 3:12). Cain is furious, and God speaks to him with unusual directness: "sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it" (Genesis 4:7). Cain does not listen. He lures his brother into a field and kills him.

When God asks where Abel is, Cain answers with one of the most famous lines in Scripture: "Am I my brother’s keeper?" (Genesis 4:9). God answers that Abel's blood is crying out from the ground. Cain is driven away, yet God puts a mark on him so that no one will kill him. Judgment and mercy again arrive together.

The chapter then follows Cain's line. They build a city, develop cattle farming, music and metalwork, so there is real human achievement here. But Lamech, a descendant, boasts to his wives that he has killed a man for wounding him, and that if Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech will be avenged seventy-sevenfold (Genesis 4:23-24). Civilization advances and so does violence.

By Genesis 6 the Lord sees that "the wickedness of man was great upon the earth" (Genesis 6:5). But even there the text adds a short sentence that points forward: Noah "found favor in the eyes of the LORD" (Genesis 6:8). The first eleven chapters of Genesis keep repeating this pattern. Sin spreads, God judges, God shows grace to someone, and the story continues.

When God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, Samuel looks at Jesse's oldest son and assumes he is the one. God corrects him with a principle that runs through the whole Bible: "the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The chosen son is David, the youngest, away tending the sheep.

David first enters Saul's court as a musician who calms the king with his harp. Then comes Goliath, the Philistine champion, nine feet tall in the traditional Hebrew text (some ancient manuscripts give a shorter height), who has been taunting the army of Israel for forty days. David goes out with a sling and five smooth stones and says to him, "You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts" (1 Samuel 17:45). The stone strikes Goliath in the forehead.

The years that follow are dangerous. Saul turns against him, and David lives as a fugitive in caves and wilderness hideouts, twice sparing Saul's life when he could have killed him. After Saul's death, David is crowned king of Judah in Hebron, and about seven years later the northern tribes also make him king. According to the book of 2 Samuel, he reigned forty years, probably from around 1010 to 970 BC. He captures the Jebusite stronghold of Jerusalem, makes it his capital, and brings the ark there.

Paul sums up David this way: God said, "I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety" (Acts 13:22). That does not mean David was without sin. It means his heart was turned toward God, as his psalms show, and that when he failed he came back in repentance.

The most troubling chapters about David come in the middle of his reign. In the spring, when kings go to war, David stays home in Jerusalem. From his roof he sees a woman bathing, finds out she is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his own soldiers, and sends for her. She becomes pregnant. David first tries to cover it up by bringing Uriah home from the front so that he will sleep with his wife, and when Uriah refuses to enjoy comforts while his men are in the field, David sends him back with a sealed letter ordering the commander to put him at the front line and withdraw. Uriah is killed.

The chapter ends with one short sentence: "the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD" (2 Samuel 11:27). God sends Nathan, who tells David a story about a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb. David is furious at the man, and Nathan says, "You are that man!" David answers with six words, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13). Nathan tells him the sin is forgiven, but the consequences will remain. The child born to Bathsheba dies, and "the sword will never depart from your house."

The cost is visible in the rest of the story: the rape of David's daughter Tamar, the murder of Amnon by Absalom, and Absalom's revolt, which sends David running from Jerusalem. Yet out of this ruin came a prayer that the church has used ever since. Psalm 51, headed as David's psalm after Nathan came to him, pleads, "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me" (Psalm 51:10).

The Israelites are camped on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, with the promised land in view. Moses is a hundred and twenty years old, and he knows he will not cross. Deuteronomy is a collection of his final speeches, a long sermon in which he reminds a new generation what God has done and calls them to love him in the land they are about to receive. The name means "second law," because Moses restates and applies the instruction given at Sinai to people who were not there to hear it.

At its heart is a short declaration Jews call the Shema, after its first word in Hebrew, "Hear." "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). The next verses tell parents to teach it to their children, to speak of it at home and on the road, to bind it on hand and forehead. Jesus quotes this passage when he is asked which commandment is greatest (Matthew 22:36-40).

Scholars have long noticed that the book's shape resembles ancient treaties between a great king and a smaller nation. It opens with a history of the relationship, lays out the terms, calls on witnesses, and ends with blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal. That fits Deuteronomy's own understanding: this is the covenant between God and Israel put into words.

The climax is a choice. Moses says that the word is not far off, and he sets before them "life and prosperity, as well as death and disaster," urging them, "choose life, so that you and your descendants may live" (Deuteronomy 30:15-19). The book ends with Moses on Mount Nebo, viewing the whole land, dying in Moab and buried by God himself, and a short verse that says no prophet since has been like him.

In the ninth century BC the northern kingdom is ruled by Ahab and his Phoenician wife Jezebel, who promote the worship of Baal, the Canaanite storm and fertility god, and who kill many of the LORD's prophets. Into this comes Elijah, a prophet from Gilead, who suddenly tells Ahab that there will be neither dew nor rain in the next years except at his word. A three-year drought follows. The contest is set up as a direct test of who controls the rain.

On Mount Carmel, Elijah faces 450 prophets of Baal before the king and the people. He tells them to prepare a bull for sacrifice and call on their god to light it, while he does the same for the LORD. The prophets of Baal shout and cut themselves from morning until evening, and nothing happens. Elijah mocks them. Then he rebuilds the altar of the LORD, soaks the offering with water three times, and prays a short prayer. Fire falls and consumes the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the water. The people fall on their faces and say, "The LORD, He is God!" (1 Kings 18:39). Then rain comes.

Elijah is not a man of steel, though. Jezebel threatens his life, and he runs into the desert and asks to die. At Mount Horeb God does not speak in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still, small voice" (1 Kings 19:12).

Elijah never dies. He is carried up to heaven in a whirlwind with a chariot of fire, and his disciple Elisha, who asks for a double share of his spirit, takes his place. Malachi's last words promise that Elijah will return before the great day of the LORD, and the New Testament says that John the Baptist came "in the spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17).

Two more men came after the first return, both with Persian authority. Ezra, a priest and scribe, led a second group to Jerusalem in 458 BC. The text says he "had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel" (Ezra 7:10). His concern was the spiritual life of the community, and he found that many had married women from the surrounding peoples and adopted their ways. The book describes a painful process of repentance.

Nehemiah, a cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, was in the palace at Susa in 445 BC when a relative told him that the walls of Jerusalem were still broken down. He wept for days and then prayed. When the king noticed his sad face and asked what he wanted, Nehemiah said a quick prayer to the God of heaven and asked to be sent to rebuild the city. The king agreed and gave him letters of passage and timber.

In Jerusalem Nehemiah inspected the ruins at night and then organized the whole population to build, each family working on the section near its home. Local rivals mocked and then threatened them, so half the men worked while the other half stood guard, with a trumpeter beside the commander. The wall was finished "in fifty-two days" (Nehemiah 6:15).

Then came the high point. On the first day of the seventh month the people gathered in the square, and Ezra stood on a wooden platform and read the Law from morning until noon, while the Levites explained its meaning. The people wept as they heard it, and then they celebrated. The prophet Malachi, whose book comes last in the Christian Old Testament, probably worked in this period. His last words promise the coming of Elijah before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5).

Numbers takes its English name from two censuses of Israel's fighting men, but it is really the story of a journey that went wrong. Israel leaves Sinai in the second year after the exodus and travels toward the promised land. At Kadesh Barnea on the southern edge of Canaan, Moses sends twelve men to explore it. They come back with grapes so large that two men carry a single cluster on a pole, and they agree that the land is rich. But ten of them add that the people there are giants and the cities are fortified. Only Caleb and Joshua say, "We must go up and take possession of the land" (Numbers 13:30).

The people weep all night and talk about choosing a new leader to take them back to Egypt. God's judgment is exact. Because they refused to enter, none of the adults aged twenty and over, except Caleb and Joshua, will see the land. One year for each day of the exploration, the nation will wander for forty years (Numbers 14:33-34). A generation dies in the desert, and their children enter instead.

The wilderness years hold other scenes: rebellions against Moses, water from a rock, a talking donkey in the story of Balaam, and a plague of snakes. When the snakes come, God tells Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, and anyone bitten who looks at it lives (Numbers 21:4-9). Jesus uses this in his talk with Nicodemus: "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life" (John 3:14-15).

Paul looks back on this generation as a warning. They all passed through the sea and ate the same spiritual food, yet most of them fell in the wilderness, and Paul says these things "took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did" (1 Corinthians 10:1-6). Numbers shows that being rescued is not the same as trusting, and that God's patience is long but real.

First Samuel opens with a woman in pain. Hannah is married to Elkanah, and she has no children. Year after year she goes to the sanctuary at Shiloh and weeps, and one year she prays so intensely that Eli the priest thinks she is drunk. She vows that if God gives her a son she will give him back. Samuel is born. When he is weaned she brings him to Shiloh to serve in the house of the LORD, and her song of thanks, which says God lifts the poor and brings down the mighty, is echoed centuries later in Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55).

Samuel grows up in a corrupt age. Eli's sons are priests who steal from the offerings, and the word of the LORD is rare. One night as a boy Samuel hears a voice, and after Eli explains who is speaking, he answers, "Speak, for Your servant is listening" (1 Samuel 3:10). Samuel becomes a prophet, a priest and the last of the judges. Israel loses a battle to the Philistines, brings out the ark of the covenant as a kind of good luck charm, and loses both the battle and the ark.

When Samuel grows old and his sons prove unworthy, the elders come to him and say, "appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations" (1 Samuel 8:5). Samuel is displeased, and God tells him the real meaning of the request: "it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king" (1 Samuel 8:7). God tells Samuel to warn them about what a king will take, from their sons, daughters, fields and flocks. They insist. The desire for a king is not wrong in itself, since God had foreseen it in Deuteronomy 17, but the motive is, because they want to be like everyone else.

Judah outlasted its northern neighbor by about a century and a half, and a few of its kings tried to turn the nation back. Hezekiah, who became king around 715 BC, removed the high places, broke the bronze serpent Moses had made, which people had begun to burn incense to, and reopened the temple. The text says that there was no one like him among the kings of Judah, "either before him or after him" (2 Kings 18:5).

In 701 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah, captured dozens of its fortified cities and surrounded Jerusalem. Hezekiah took the threatening letter into the temple, spread it out before the LORD and prayed. According to Kings, the angel of the LORD struck down the Assyrian camp in one night, and Sennacherib went home. Sennacherib's own prism records that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage" but does not say he took the city. In preparation for the siege Hezekiah had dug a tunnel to bring water from the Gihon spring inside the walls, and an inscription from it was found in 1880.

The other great reformer was Josiah, who became king at eight years old and was about twenty-six when workmen repairing the temple found "the Book of the Law" (2 Kings 22:8). Most scholars think it was Deuteronomy or part of it. When it was read to him, he tore his clothes, led a nationwide reform, destroyed idols, and kept a Passover such as had not been held since the time of the judges. The writer says that no king before or after "turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength" (2 Kings 23:25).
Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BC, fighting Pharaoh Neco. The reforms had not reached the heart of the people. Within a generation Judah was finished.

The Bible opens with a claim that was bold in its own day: one God made everything, and he did it by speaking. Genesis 1:1 gives the heading, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." The rest of the chapter unpacks it, day by day, in a careful and almost liturgical pattern. God separates light from darkness, sea from sky, sea from dry land, then fills each realm: lights in the sky, fish and birds, land animals, and finally human beings.

Other ancient peoples told stories of creation too, and often the world came out of a battle between gods, or from the body of a slain deity. Genesis tells it differently. There is no rival. The sun and moon, which many nations worshiped, are simply lamps that God hangs in the sky. Nothing in the created order is divine, and nothing is an accident.

At the end of each stage God calls what he has made good, and after the people appear the text says, "indeed, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Matter is not evil. Bodies, food, work, marriage, rest and beauty are all part of the original design. Human beings are made in the image of God and given a task: to rule over the creation, which in the Bible means to look after it as a king looks after a land he loves (Genesis 1:26-28).

Christians have long argued about how to read the days of Genesis 1: as six ordinary days, as long ages, as a literary frame, or in other ways. Those debates are real, but they should not hide what every reading holds in common. The world has a Maker, the Maker is good, and people have a purpose in it.
in-the-beginning-a-world-made-on-purpose.q: What difference does it make to say the world was made on purpose and called good?

b: Isaiah of Jerusalem served as a prophet for roughly forty years from about 740 BC, in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. His call comes in one of the great scenes of Scripture. In the year King Uzziah dies, he sees the Lord seated on a high throne, with the train of his robe filling the temple, and seraphim calling to one another, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory" (Isaiah 6:3). The doorposts shake. Isaiah says, "Woe is me, for I am ruined." A seraph touches his lips with a glowing coal from the altar, and then he hears the Lord asking, "Whom shall I send?" and answers, "Here am I. Send me!"

The sixty-six chapters of the book move between judgment on Judah and its neighbors and promises of a future king and a future world. Isaiah says that "the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son" named Immanuel, God with us (Isaiah 7:14), and that a child will be born whose names are "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6). He describes a time when the nations will stream to Zion to learn God's ways, and they "will beat their swords into plowshares" (Isaiah 2:2-4).

From chapter 40 the tone turns to comfort, and a figure called the Servant of the LORD appears. In chapter 53 the Servant is "pierced for our transgressions" and "the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all." The New Testament quotes Isaiah more than any other prophet, and Philip uses this chapter to explain Jesus to an Ethiopian official (Acts 8:26-35).

Most scholars of earlier generations took the whole book as the work of one prophet, and many Christians still do. Many modern scholars think chapters 40 to 66 were written by a later author, or authors, during or after the exile. Both camps agree on the book's final shape and on its message: God is holy, he judges, and he will save.

The northern kingdom of Israel lasted about two hundred years, from the split around 931 BC to its fall in 722 BC. None of its nineteen kings is said to have done what was right. During its last decades the great power of the region was Assyria, a brutal empire based in Nineveh, which collected tribute from smaller nations and deported those who rebelled.

God sent prophets to the north in these years. Amos, a shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah, went to Bethel and denounced the rich for selling the needy for a pair of sandals. The priest there told him to go home and prophesy in his own country, and Amos replied that he was no professional prophet, just a herdsman, and that the LORD had taken him and told him to go. Hosea, whose wife left him for other lovers, was told to take her back as a picture of God's faithfulness to unfaithful Israel. In a verse Matthew later applies to the child Jesus, God says through Hosea, "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son" (Hosea 11:1). Jonah, active in the first half of the same century, was sent to Nineveh itself.

The end came in 722 BC. After a siege of about three years, Samaria, the capital, fell to the Assyrian king, and large numbers of its people were deported to other parts of the empire. Others were brought in to settle the land, and their descendants mixed with those who remained, which is part of the background to the later tensions between Jews and Samaritans.

The writer of 2 Kings gives the cause in one long, sorrowful paragraph. The people had "rejected His statutes and the covenant He had made with their fathers," despite the warnings of every prophet (2 Kings 17:13-18). The ten tribes of the north never returned as a nation. Only Judah, and Jerusalem with David's house, remained.

Isaac and Rebekah have twin sons, Esau and Jacob, and before they are born God tells Rebekah that the older will serve the younger. Jacob's name means "heel-grabber" or "deceiver," and he lives up to it. He buys Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew and with his mother's help tricks his father into giving him the blessing. He flees from his furious brother, and the first night alone he dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down and the LORD standing at the top, repeating to him the promise made to Abraham (Genesis 28:10-17).

Jacob then spends twenty years in Haran, where his uncle Laban deceives him in turn. He marries Leah and Rachel, and the two women and their maids bear him twelve sons and a daughter. Returning home, he is afraid to meet Esau, and the night before the meeting he wrestles with a man until daybreak. He refuses to let go until the man blesses him, and he leaves with a limp and a new name: Israel, which the text explains this way: "you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed" (Genesis 32:28). He had spent his whole life grasping, and now God would give him what he could not grasp.

The twelve sons are Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin, and their families become the tribes of Israel. Joseph's share is later divided between his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. The whole people take their name from Jacob, so Israel is the family of a man who struggled with God.

The patriarchs are no saints, and the Bible does not clean them up. Abraham lies, Isaac favors one son, Jacob schemes. The promise is carried by a God who keeps his word, not by the goodness of the people who receive it.

Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, near Jerusalem. He was called young, around 627 BC, and told that God had known him before he was formed in the womb. He protested that he was only a boy, and God replied that he would put his words in Jeremiah's mouth. The task was hard: "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant" (Jeremiah 1:10). For about forty years he warned that Babylon would come, and he was beaten, put in stocks, thrown into a cistern and accused of treason.

He is sometimes called the weeping prophet, and the title fits. He loved the people he condemned. When the first Judeans were taken to Babylon in 597 BC he wrote them a letter telling them to build houses, plant gardens, seek the welfare of the city where they now lived and wait. "When Babylon's seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place" (Jeremiah 29:10). The verse that follows, "For I know the plans I have for you," was spoken to exiles, and its promise is of a future after long waiting.

His great word of hope is in chapter 31. The old covenant, made at Sinai, was one "they broke." God will make a new one: "I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people." Everyone will know him, "from the least of them to the greatest," and he will "forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more" (Jeremiah 31:31-34).

At the Last Supper Jesus lifted a cup and said, "This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you" (Luke 22:20). The letter to the Hebrews quotes the whole passage and says the new covenant has arrived (Hebrews 8:7-13).

The last quarter of Genesis follows Jacob's favorite son. Joseph is loved by his father, given a richly ornamented robe, and has dreams that his family will bow down to him. His brothers, burning with jealousy, sell him to traders heading for Egypt and tell their father he has been killed. Joseph becomes a slave in the house of Potiphar, is falsely accused by Potiphar's wife, and ends up in prison.

In prison he correctly interprets the dreams of two of Pharaoh's officials, and two years later, when Pharaoh himself has a troubling dream, he is called out. Joseph explains that seven good years will be followed by seven years of famine and recommends storing grain. Pharaoh makes him second in command of Egypt. When the famine comes, it reaches Canaan, and Joseph's brothers arrive to buy grain. They do not recognize him. After testing them, Joseph weeps and tells them who he is.

The center of the story is his statement to them after their father dies and they fear revenge: "what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this," which was "to preserve the lives of many people" (Genesis 50:20). It does not say that the evil was good. It says that God was working through it for a larger purpose, and that is the idea behind Paul's later words in Romans 8:28.

The story also answers a plain question: how did the family of Abraham, living in Canaan, end up in Egypt? Famine drove them there, and Joseph's position made it possible. Jacob's family settles in the region of Goshen and grows into a nation. The book ends with Joseph's coffin in Egypt and a promise that God will bring them back to the land.

Joshua, Moses' assistant, takes the lead and crosses the Jordan with the people. God tells him three times to be strong and courageous, and to keep the book of the law on his lips. The first city is Jericho, and the way it falls is strange. For six days the army marches once around the walls in silence, with seven priests carrying trumpets and the ark. On the seventh day they march seven times, the trumpets sound, the people shout, and the wall collapses (Joshua 6).

Before that, two spies had stayed in the house of a woman named Rahab, a Canaanite. She tells them that her people have heard what God did at the Red Sea and that she believes "the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below" (Joshua 2:11). She helps them escape, and she and her family are spared. She later appears in the family tree of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), and Hebrews commends her faith.

The book then describes campaigns in the central, southern and northern parts of the land, and the dividing of territory among the tribes. It says plainly that Canaanite cities were to be put under the ban, a Hebrew term for being devoted to destruction, as an act of judgment on peoples whose sins God had been waiting out for centuries (compare Genesis 15:16). This is the hardest material in the book to read. Christians have taken it in different ways. Some stress that this was a unique, time-bound judgment that cannot serve as a pattern for any later war. Some argue that the language is partly stylized and that the text elsewhere says the peoples were not fully driven out. All agree that no New Testament writer treats it as a model for how Christians should deal with their neighbors.

Joshua ends with a gathering at Shechem where the old leader tells the people, "choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve," and then adds, "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15).

Twenty-one of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament are letters. They were written in the first generation of the church, in most cases by apostles, to congregations or individuals facing particular problems, and they make up the oldest part of the New Testament. Among the earliest are James, Galatians and 1 Thessalonians, written in the late 40s and early 50s AD, before the Gospels as we have them were finished.

Thirteen letters bear the name of Paul. Some are addressed to churches (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians), and four to individuals (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon). Hebrews has no named author. The rest are called the general letters because they are addressed to wider circles: James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John, and Jude.

Each letter has a particular occasion. Paul writes to Corinth because the church is divided and tolerating immorality. He writes to Galatia because teachers are insisting that Gentiles must keep the law. He writes to Philippi to thank them for their gift. Yet it is striking how much of the letters is about the same things: the person and work of Christ, the gospel, new life in the Spirit, love, holiness, hope, and the shape of the community. Peter writes to scattered believers who are suffering, reminding them that they have "a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3).

Nearly all the doctrine in the next course of this library, on theology, rests on these letters. They were occasional documents, but the church recognized in them the voice of God to every generation. Paul tells Timothy that "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16).

Leviticus is the book most readers abandon, and that is a loss, because it answers a hard question: if God has just moved into the middle of a camp of sinners, how do they stay alive? The tabernacle is finished at the end of Exodus. Leviticus opens with God speaking to Moses from it, and the rest of the book explains how the people can come near.

The first seven chapters list five kinds of offering. The burnt offering is given wholly to God and pictures complete devotion. The grain offering is a gift of the first fruits of the harvest. The peace offering is a shared meal. The sin offering and guilt offering deal with wrongs, one with sin as a condition and one with specific debts that need paying back. In each case a worshiper lays a hand on the animal, the animal dies in the worshiper's place, and the priest carries out the ritual.

The middle chapters cover the priesthood, clean and unclean animals, skin diseases, bodily discharges and the great Day of Atonement. The second half applies holiness to ordinary life: honest scales, fair wages, care for the poor, respect for the old. The refrain is "be holy, because I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44). Hidden in the middle of this is the verse Jesus calls the second great commandment: "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18).

The book also shows the limits of the system. The same sacrifices had to be offered again and again. The letter to the Hebrews says that the law was only "a shadow of the good things to come" and that the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sins (Hebrews 10:1-4). Leviticus therefore creates a longing it cannot fill. It teaches Israel that sin is serious, that atonement costs a life, and that only God can provide a way home. Christians read it as the vocabulary in which the cross is explained.
leviticus-how-a-holy-god-lives-with-sinf.q: Why would a holy God give his people so many instructions about sacrifice and cleanness?

b: Exodus begins several centuries after Genesis ends. The family of Jacob has grown into a large people, and a new king "who did not know Joseph" fears them and turns them into slaves, working on brick and mortar. When that does not stop their growth, he orders every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile. One mother hides her son in a basket among the reeds, and Pharaoh's own daughter finds and raises him. He is named Moses.

At eighty Moses is a shepherd in the wilderness of Midian when he sees a bush that burns without burning up. God speaks from it, tells him he has seen the misery of his people, and sends him to Pharaoh. Moses objects, and asks God's name. The answer is "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14), which is tied to the Hebrew four-letter name YHWH, usually written "the LORD" in English Bibles.

Ten plagues fall on Egypt, and the last, the death of the firstborn, is the one that breaks Pharaoh. Before it, God tells each Hebrew household to kill a lamb, put its blood on the doorposts, and eat a meal in haste. When the destroyer passes through, he will pass over every house with the blood. That night is the first Passover. Israel leaves, Pharaoh chases them, and at the sea the water divides so that they cross on dry ground and the pursuing army is drowned.

When the date is considered, scholars divide between an early exodus around 1446 BC, based on 1 Kings 6:1, and a later one around 1260 BC, based on archaeological evidence from the Egyptian capital Pi-Ramesses. The Bible's own emphasis is not on the date. It is on the fact that God hears, comes down, and saves. Paul says that "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7), which is why Christians keep reading the exodus as the pattern of their own deliverance.

God sees that the earth is filled with violence, and he tells Noah that he will end it. At the same time he tells him how to be saved: build a large vessel, an ark, and bring in his family and pairs of the animals. Noah does exactly as he is told, which the author notes more than once. When the flood has come and gone, and the ark has settled, Noah steps out onto dry ground and builds an altar. God smells the pleasing aroma and says in his heart, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth" (Genesis 8:21).

That is a remarkable verse. The reason God gives for sparing the world is the same reason he gave for destroying it. The flood has not fixed human hearts, and God knows that. So he makes a promise instead: he establishes a covenant with Noah, with his descendants and with every living creature, that never again will a flood destroy the earth. The sign is the rainbow, set in the clouds. The Hebrew word for the rainbow is the ordinary word for a warrior's bow, as if God had hung up his weapon in the clouds.

Readers disagree about the extent of the flood. Some hold it was global, some regional to the area known to the early writers, and the scholarly literature on ancient flood stories (such as the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh and the Atrahasis story) shows both parallels and sharp differences. What stands out in Genesis is how the story is told: a moral holiness at the center, a God who judges and saves, and the first formal covenant of the Bible. Peter later sees the water as a picture of baptism, through which believers are saved (1 Peter 3:20-21).

The Bible is a library, not a single book. It has sixty-six books written over roughly 1,500 years by many different authors: shepherds, kings, fishermen, a tax collector, a physician, a tentmaker. They wrote in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, in laws and poems, in letters and battle reports and visions. Yet Christians have always read it as one continuous story with a single author behind the human ones.

The story moves in four great movements. It begins with creation, a good world made by a good God, with people made to know him and to look after what he made. Then comes the fall, when the first humans turn away from God and everything is damaged: relationships, work, bodies, the ground itself. The longest part of the Bible is redemption, the account of how God sets out to rescue what was lost, first through a family, then a nation, then a single person, Jesus. The story ends with new creation, where the damage is undone and God lives with his people again.

Jesus himself taught that the Old Testament was pointing to him. On the road to Emmaus, after his resurrection, he took two confused disciples through "Moses and all the Prophets" and explained what the Scriptures said about himself (Luke 24:27). That is the key for reading everything else. A single psalm or a single battle may look like an isolated scene, but each one sits somewhere on this map, and learning to find the place on the map is most of what a seminary course in the Bible teaches.
The lessons in this course walk the story in order, from the first page to the last, and then pull out the threads that run through the whole thing.
one-story-in-sixty-six-books.q: If someone asked you what the whole Bible is about, how would you answer in two sentences?

b: For forty days after his resurrection Jesus appeared to his followers, speaking about the kingdom of God, and then he ascended into heaven. Before leaving, he told them to wait in Jerusalem for the gift the Father had promised, and then said, "you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth" (Acts 1:8).

Ten days later was Pentecost, the Jewish feast of weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Jews from all over the empire were in Jerusalem. The disciples were together in one place, and "suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven." Tongues like flames of fire rested on each of them, and they began to speak "in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them" (Acts 2:2-4). The crowd heard the message in their own languages, and some mocked, saying that the disciples were drunk.

Peter stood up and explained. This, he said, was what the prophet Joel had foretold, that God would pour out his Spirit on all people. He preached that Jesus of Nazareth, whom they had crucified, God had raised and made both Lord and Messiah. The crowd was cut to the heart, and asked what to do. Peter said, "Repent and be baptized," and about three thousand were added that day (Acts 2:38,41).

The new community met daily for the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. They shared their goods with anyone in need. The rest of Acts tells how this small group in one city grew, in about thirty years, into churches in cities across the empire. The Spirit who came on that day is the one who gathers and empowers the church still.

Ruth begins "in the days when the judges ruled," and so it is a small window of light in an otherwise dark age. A famine drives Elimelech and Naomi from Bethlehem to Moab, where their two sons marry Moabite women. Then the men all die, and Naomi is left a widow with two daughters-in-law. She decides to go home. One daughter-in-law, Orpah, turns back. The other, Ruth, clings to her and says, "wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16).

In Bethlehem the two women are destitute, and Ruth goes into the barley fields to pick up the leftover grain that the law allowed the poor to gather. By God's providence she lands in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's dead husband, who treats her with extraordinary kindness. Following Naomi's plan, Ruth later lies down at Boaz's feet on the threshing floor and asks him to spread his cloak over her.

Boaz is what Israelite law called a kinsman-redeemer, the Hebrew go'el: a close relative who could buy back family land and marry a widow to preserve her husband's line. At the town gate he deals with a nearer relative who passes on the duty, and then he marries Ruth. They have a son, Obed, who becomes the grandfather of David.

The last lines of the book give the genealogy. A Moabite woman, a foreigner from a people Israel had good reasons to distrust, stands in the family line of the greatest king, and so in the line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Ruth shows that the promise to Abraham was always meant for outsiders, and that God's redeemer is a relative who pays what is owed to bring a stranger home.

Saul looks like a king. He is the son of a wealthy man from the tribe of Benjamin, handsome, and a head taller than anyone else in Israel. He is out looking for lost donkeys when he meets Samuel, who anoints him privately with oil, and later he is chosen by lot at Mizpah, where Saul is found hiding among the baggage. His early reign goes well. He rescues the town of Jabesh Gilead from an Ammonite threat, and the people shout for joy.

The trouble begins with two failures of obedience. In 1 Samuel 13 the Philistine army is gathering at Gilgal, Samuel has not come at the appointed time, and Saul, with his men beginning to scatter, offers the sacrifice himself, which was a priest's task. Samuel arrives and tells him that his kingdom will not last: "the LORD has sought a man after His own heart" (1 Samuel 13:14). Later God tells Saul to destroy the Amalekites completely, and Saul spares their king and the best of the animals, then claims he kept them to sacrifice. Samuel's answer is one of the great sentences in the Bible: "obedience is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22).

After this the Spirit of the LORD leaves Saul, and a tormenting spirit troubles him. He becomes jealous and paranoid, especially of David, and spends years hunting a man who has done him no wrong. He consults a medium on the night before his final battle, and dies on Mount Gilboa by his own sword, together with his sons including Jonathan.
Saul's story is a warning about outward success without inward trust. He has the right look, the right start and the Spirit's help for a while, but he cannot bring himself to obey.

Three months after leaving Egypt, the Israelites camp at the foot of Mount Sinai. God tells Moses what to say. He reminds them what he did to Egypt, and then adds: "if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations." They are to be "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:5-6). Notice the order. God saves first. The law comes after the rescue, not before it.

Then, amid thunder, fire and a trumpet blast, God speaks the Ten Commandments to the whole assembly. They start with the relationship (no other gods, no images, no misuse of the name, the Sabbath) and move to the community (honor parents, no murder, adultery, theft, false witness, coveting). Moses then gives them a longer set of laws, and the people reply, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient." Moses seals the covenant by sprinkling blood on the altar and on the people (Exodus 24:3-8).

The Mosaic covenant gave Israel a constitution, a worship, and a way of life that set them apart from their neighbors. Christians differ on how the law applies today. A common view in the Reformed tradition divides it into moral, civil and ceremonial parts and holds that only the moral law still binds. Others stress that the whole law is fulfilled in Christ and that believers are under the law of Christ. Jesus said, "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them" (Matthew 5:17).
Paul adds that the law acted as a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). It showed what holiness looked like, exposed sin, and pointed to a need that only a savior could meet.

Solomon becomes king after David and, early in his reign, goes to Gibeon to offer sacrifices. That night God appears to him in a dream and says, "Ask, and I will give it to you!" Solomon asks for a discerning heart to judge the people. God is so pleased that he adds the wealth and honor Solomon did not ask for. The wisdom is soon put to the test in the famous case of two women and one living baby, and in the years that follow Solomon is known across the ancient world for his proverbs and songs.

His greatest project is the temple in Jerusalem. According to 1 Kings 6:1, he began it in the fourth year of his reign, which most calculate as about 966 BC, and it took seven years to complete. It was built on the hill north of David's city, modeled on the tabernacle's plan but on a much grander scale, with cedar from Lebanon and gold overlay. At its dedication the ark was placed in the inner room, and a cloud filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister. Solomon's prayer asks, "will God indeed dwell upon the earth? The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built" (1 Kings 8:27).

The ending is sad. Solomon marries many foreign women, and as he grows old they turn his heart toward other gods. He builds high places for the gods of his wives. God tells him that the kingdom will be torn from his son. A man who began by asking for wisdom ended by ignoring the very law the king was told to copy and read, which warned against many wives and many horses (Deuteronomy 17:16-17).

David is settled in his palace in Jerusalem, and he feels uncomfortable that the ark of God sits in a tent. He tells the prophet Nathan that he wants to build a house for God. Nathan first says go ahead, then that night God corrects him with a message that turns the whole idea upside down. David wants to build God a house. God says that he will build David a house, meaning a dynasty.

The promise in 2 Samuel 7 has several parts. God will make David's name great. He will give Israel a secure home. He will raise up one of David's descendants after him, who will build a house for God's name. And then comes the center: "I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever" (2 Samuel 7:13). God adds that he will be a father to that son, and if the son does wrong, God will discipline him, but "My loving devotion will never be removed" as it was from Saul (2 Samuel 7:15).

This covenant becomes the foundation of the hope for a Messiah, a word that means "anointed one." After the kingdom divides, falls and goes into exile, the prophets keep returning to the promise: a future king from David's line who will rule with justice and peace. The Psalms recall it (Psalm 89), and Isaiah and Jeremiah and Ezekiel and Micah all depend on it.

The New Testament opens with it. Matthew's first line calls Jesus "the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). When the angel appears to Mary, he says that her son will be given "the throne of His father David," and that "His kingdom will never end" (Luke 1:32-33). The apostles preach the resurrection as the proof that God has set this king on his throne.

All four Gospels spend a disproportionate share of their space on the last week of Jesus' life, and the cross stands at the center. Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey while crowds shouted hosanna, overturned the tables in the temple, taught in its courts, and shared a Passover meal with his disciples on Thursday night. He was betrayed by Judas, arrested in the garden of Gethsemane, tried by the Jewish council and by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, and sentenced to death by crucifixion, which was a Roman form of public execution for slaves and rebels.

Jesus had said ahead of time what it meant: "even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). On the cross he was mocked, darkness fell for three hours at midday, and he cried out in the words of Psalm 22. After a loud cry he died, and the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom. The Roman centurion said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39).

The year is debated. Most scholars say the crucifixion happened on a Friday at Passover, either in AD 30 or AD 33, with a strong majority favoring one of those two. The New Testament, however, cares more about the meaning than the date. Paul writes that "God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8).

The church has never had a single official theory of how the cross saves. Christians describe it as a ransom, a victory over the powers of evil, a sacrifice for sin, a substitute taking the penalty, and an example of love. All of them point to the one fact that the earliest preachers placed first: that "Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3).

Judges covers the long stretch between Joshua and the first king, and it is one of the bleakest books in the Bible. The writer explains the pattern in chapter 2. After Joshua's generation dies, a new generation arises "who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel" (Judges 2:10). The people start worshiping the Baals, the local gods of Canaan, and the LORD gives them into the hand of raiders and oppressors. They cry out, God raises up a judge to rescue them, and while the judge lives there is peace. Then the judge dies, and the people sink back lower than before.

That cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, rescue and rest repeats at least six times, and each repetition is worse. The judges themselves decline. Othniel and Ehud are clear heroes. Deborah is a prophet who leads with Barak and wins a famous victory. Gideon starts as a timid man threshing wheat in a winepress, defeats an army with three hundred men and torches in jars, and then makes a golden object that becomes a snare. Jephthah makes a tragic vow. Samson, set apart from birth as a Nazirite, is a man of enormous strength and almost no self-control, who dies bringing down a temple on himself and on the Philistines.

The book closes with two ghastly stories of idolatry and violence within Israel itself, and with a sentence repeated in the last chapter: "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25).

That line sets up what follows. Israel needs more than a series of temporary rescuers. It needs a king who will lead faithfully, and ultimately a deliverer whose rescue does not wear off when he dies.
the-cycle-of-the-judges.q: Where do you see the cycle of Judges in your own life or in the culture around you?

b: Once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the high priest of Israel did something no one else could do. He passed through the curtain and entered the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant stood beneath the golden mercy seat. Leviticus 16 gives the whole procedure, and it is a study in how seriously the Bible takes the gap between God and sinful people.

The high priest first washed and put on plain linen. He offered a bull for his own sin, since he was a sinner too. He took a censer of burning coals and incense into the inner room, so that a cloud of smoke covered the mercy seat. He then sprinkled the blood of the bull there, and afterward the blood of a goat chosen "for the LORD" for the sins of the people. Blood was applied to the sanctuary itself, because even the holy place was affected by the uncleanness of those who used it.

Then came a second goat. The priest laid both hands on its head and confessed over it all the sins of Israel. The goat was led away into the wilderness, and it carried on itself all their iniquities to a solitary land (Leviticus 16:22). That is the origin of the word scapegoat in English. People were told to "afflict" themselves, which Jews have always understood as fasting, and to do no work. The day is still observed in Judaism as Yom Kippur.

The letter to the Hebrews reads the day as a picture. Christ entered not an earthly tent but heaven itself, not with the blood of goats but with his own, and not once a year but once for all (Hebrews 9:11-12). Because of that, the writer says, believers can "draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith" (Hebrews 10:22). The way past the curtain is open.

In 605 BC Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish and became the dominant power of the Near East. Under Nebuchadnezzar it moved against Judah. In 597 BC, after a short siege, the young king Jehoiachin surrendered, and Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon along with thousands of the leading people, including the priest Ezekiel. He put Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah on the throne. Zedekiah rebelled, against Jeremiah's repeated warning, and the army came again.

The siege of Jerusalem lasted about eighteen months. In the summer of 586 BC the walls were breached. Zedekiah tried to escape at night, was caught, and was made to watch his sons killed before he was blinded and taken to Babylon in chains. Then Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, came to the city: "He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem" (2 Kings 25:9). The walls were torn down, the temple's bronze and gold carried away, and most of the people who survived were deported. The poorest were left to farm the land.

The date is given as 586 BC in many books and 587 BC in others, depending on how the Babylonian and Judean calendars are reconciled. What matters is what ended. The land, the city, the temple, the kingdom of David and the whole structure through which Israel knew God's presence were gone.

The book of Lamentations is the poetry of that grief. In the middle of it the writer says, "Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed" (Lamentations 3:21-22). The prophet Habakkuk, who had seen it coming, said that even if the fig tree does not bloom and the fields produce no food, "yet I will exult in the LORD" (Habakkuk 3:17-18).

Genesis 3 is the shortest and most consequential chapter in the Bible. A serpent asks the woman a question designed to make God look stingy: "Did God really say, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden?'" (Genesis 3:1). It twists what God said, then contradicts it outright, then offers the thing that has tempted every human since: you can be like God. The woman looks at the fruit, sees that it is good for food and pleasing to the eye, takes it, and gives some to her husband, who is with her.

Notice what happens at once. They discover they are naked and hide. For the first time they feel shame. When God comes walking in the garden, they hide from him, and when he asks what happened, the man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent. In a few verses the first marriage and the first friendship with God have both cracked.

The rest of the Bible reads this as the original wound. Paul writes that "sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin" (Romans 5:12). Creation itself "was subjected to futility" and waits to be set free (Romans 8:20-21). Christians call this the fall, and the doctrine of sin grows out of it: we are born into a world and a nature already bent away from God.

Traditions differ on exactly how the effects of that first sin pass down to everyone. Some speak of inherited guilt, some of an inherited corruption and a deadly inheritance, and the Eastern churches stress mortality more than guilt. All of them agree on the main fact. Something went badly wrong at the start, and people cannot repair it by themselves. That is why the rest of the story is a rescue.

When God finds the man and the woman hiding, he does not simply condemn them. He first judges the serpent, and in doing so he makes a promise: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel" (Genesis 3:15). The woman's descendants will fight the serpent's, and one of them will strike a fatal blow at the head while suffering a wound at the heel.

Christians have long read this verse as the first announcement of the gospel, and the Latin name protoevangelium means exactly that, the first gospel. Irenaeus, a bishop in Gaul writing about AD 180, read the promised offspring as Christ, and many later writers followed him. Others hold that the verse speaks first of the ongoing conflict between humanity and evil, and that the New Testament shows that conflict reaching its climax in Jesus. Either way, the shape fits. At the cross the serpent's seed strikes the heel of the woman's offspring, and the resurrection crushes the head of death. As John puts it, "This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8).

A smaller sign comes a few verses later. God makes garments of skin for the man and the woman and clothes them himself (Genesis 3:21). Something had to die to cover their shame. The tone is gentle, but the pattern is already there and will grow: sin is serious, life is costly, and God himself provides the covering.
The point to carry forward is that the Bible's story of rescue starts in the same chapter as the story of the fall. God did not wait for people to ask for help. He spoke the promise first.

Between the last words of Malachi, around 430 BC, and the first words about John the Baptist, there are roughly four hundred years in which the Bible records no new prophetic voice. Protestants call this the intertestamental period, and it was anything but quiet. The Persian empire gave way to Alexander the Great, who swept through the region in 333 and 332 BC, and after his early death his generals split his empire. Judea was caught between two of those kingdoms, the Ptolemies in Egypt and the Seleucids in Syria.

Greek language and culture spread everywhere. In Alexandria in Egypt, in the third century BC, Jewish scholars began translating their Scriptures into Greek, producing what is called the Septuagint, which is the Bible the apostles often quote. Then in 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes tried to force the Jews to give up their religion. He banned circumcision and the Sabbath, and set up an altar to Zeus in the temple. A priest named Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees, started a revolt. Judas Maccabeus recaptured Jerusalem and rededicated the temple in 164 BC, which Jews still remember at Hanukkah.

For about a century the Maccabee family, called the Hasmoneans, ruled an independent Jewish state. Then Rome arrived. General Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, and the Roman senate had named Herod, an Idumean, king of the Jews in 40 BC, though he took Jerusalem only in 37 BC. Herod rebuilt the temple on a magnificent scale. Along the way, groups such as the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes formed, and later the Zealots, each with its own idea of how to be faithful.

Through all of it the Jews looked for the fulfillment of the promises: a Messiah, a new covenant, a kingdom. They were back in the land, but under foreign rule. The world was waiting without knowing exactly for what.

Genesis 2 retells the sixth day from close up. God shapes a man out of the dust of the ground and breathes life into him. The Hebrew sounds almost like a pun: the man is adam, and the ground is adamah. He is earth and he is breath, both at once. God plants a garden in Eden and puts the man there "to cultivate and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). Work is therefore not a punishment. It is part of paradise.

In the middle of the garden stand two trees: the tree of life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. God gives one command with one warning. The man may eat from every tree except the second, "for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die" (Genesis 2:17). The command is simple, and that is the point. It gives the man something to trust God about, a way to say yes to being a creature who depends on his Maker.

Then God makes an observation that surprises the reader: "It is not good for the man to be alone" (Genesis 2:18). Everything so far has been good, and now something is lacking. God brings the woman as a partner, and the man answers with the first poem in the Bible. The chapter closes with a picture of a man and his wife who are naked and feel no shame, at ease with each other and with God.

Readers differ on how to take the details of Genesis 2 and 3. Some read the garden, the trees and the serpent as plain history, some as rich symbols of real events, and some as a story that teaches truth in a literary form. What the whole church has held in common is that this is the starting point for everything that follows: the first people were made good, placed in a home with God, and given a choice.

At first the followers of Jesus were all Jews, and many assumed they would stay a movement within Judaism. But persecution after the death of Stephen scattered them, and wherever they went they told the story. Philip preached to the Samaritans, who had been despised by Jews for centuries, and many believed. Then Peter went to the house of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, and saw the Holy Spirit fall on non-Jews as he spoke. "I now truly understand," Peter said, "that God does not show favoritism" (Acts 10:34).

In Antioch, the third largest city in the empire, believers began to speak to Greeks as well as Jews, and a large number turned to the Lord. It was there, Acts says, that "the disciples were first called Christians" (Acts 11:26). The church at Antioch sent out Barnabas and Saul, who is also called Paul, on a mission to the island of Cyprus and then to the interior of what is now Turkey. Paul made three major journeys over about a decade, planting churches in cities such as Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus.

The great controversy was whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. About AD 49 the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem to decide. Peter argued that God "made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith," and that "we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are" (Acts 15:9,11). James agreed, and the church sent a letter. Gentiles would be accepted by faith, without circumcision.

Paul later put the new situation in a sentence: in Christ there is "neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female" (Galatians 3:28). The promise to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed, was starting to come true.

Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" (Luke 3:1), which is about AD 28 or 29. Jesus came to be baptized by John, heard the Father's voice from heaven, was tested for forty days in the wilderness, and then began to teach. Mark gives the headline of his preaching: "The time is fulfilled," He said, "and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!" (Mark 1:15).

The kingdom of God is the central subject of Jesus' teaching, and it is easy to misunderstand. It is not a place in the sky, and it is not simply a feeling inside. It is God's kingly rule, the reign that the prophets had promised, breaking into the world in the person of Jesus. When he heals the sick, drives out demons, forgives sins and eats with outcasts, these are the signs that the king has come. He teaches the disciples to pray, "Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10).

In Nazareth he reads from the scroll of Isaiah about good news for the poor, freedom for prisoners and sight for the blind, and then says, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21). His stories, the parables, tell of seeds and treasure and a wedding feast, saying that the kingdom starts small and grows, costs everything and is a gift, and has already begun although its fullness is still to come.

Jesus chose twelve disciples, a number that many readers connect with the twelve tribes of Israel. His public ministry lasted something like three years. Most Christians hold that the kingdom has come in Jesus, is spreading through the church, and will be completed when he returns.

After Solomon's death around 931 BC, his son Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be crowned by all Israel. The northern tribes ask him to ease the heavy labor and taxes of his father's reign. The older advisors tell him to give them a kind answer. The young men he grew up with tell him to say, "Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke." Rehoboam takes the second advice, and the north responds with a cry that echoes David's earlier rebellion: "To your tents, O Israel!" (1 Kings 12:16).

The nation breaks into two kingdoms. The ten northern tribes call themselves Israel, with Jeroboam as their king. The two southern tribes, Judah and Benjamin, remain loyal to David's family, and are called Judah, with Jerusalem as their capital. A prophet had told Jeroboam beforehand that God would do this because of Solomon's idolatry, and had promised him a lasting dynasty if he would keep God's ways.

Jeroboam is afraid that if his people keep going to the temple in Jerusalem to worship, they will return to Rehoboam. So he sets up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan, the southern and northern ends of his territory, and says, "Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (1 Kings 12:28). He also creates a new priesthood and a new festival. The charge that follows him through the rest of Kings is that later northern kings repeated the sin of Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin.

Every northern king after him is judged to have done evil, and none of the dynasties lasts long. The southern kings are a mixture, with a few faithful rulers among many unfaithful ones, but David's line continues without a break until the exile.

The Bible ends where it began, in a garden, but a garden that has grown into a city. The last two chapters of Revelation, written by John from the island of Patmos about AD 95 according to the most common view, describe the goal of the whole story. John sees "a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away" (Revelation 21:1). The holy city, the new Jerusalem, comes down out of heaven from God, "prepared as a bride adorned for her husband."

Then he hears the central announcement: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God." The tabernacle, the temple and the incarnation have all led here, to God living with his people. "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes," and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain. The One on the throne says, "Behold, I make all things new."

Almost every feature reverses something from the early chapters of Genesis. The river of the water of life flows through the city, and on both sides stands the tree of life, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations. "No longer will there be any curse." There is no night. God's servants "will see His face," which no one could do after Eden, and they "will reign forever and ever" (Revelation 22:3-5).

Christians differ on how literally to read the images, and on the order of events leading up to this point, which the course on theology takes up. But there is wide agreement about the destination. The story does not end with souls floating off to a distant heaven. It ends with the renewal of creation and the presence of God among his people, and Paul can say that the sufferings of the present are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed (Romans 8:18).
